A Computer Engineering student’s thoughts on learning, writing code, and using AI without skipping the fundamentals.

4 min read
Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

I’m a Computer Engineering student about to begin my fourth year. During my studies, I have worked with languages such as Java, C, C++, and C#. Although these languages helped me build a foundation in programming, artificial intelligence has always been the field that interested me the most.
I wanted to understand what happens behind the tools we use every day. How does a machine learn from data? How are predictions made? What separates a model that works from one that does not?
Instead of trying to learn everything at once, I decided to start with the foundations. That is how I began Atil Samancioglu’s Data Science and Machine Learning course.
Learning in Two Places at Once
Press enter or click to view image in full size

My study method may seem a little traditional. I keep a physical notebook next to my computer and write down important concepts by hand. At the same time, I practise the code on my computer.
Writing on paper slows me down in a useful way. It forces me to think about what I have just learned instead of immediately moving on to the next lesson. Coding on the computer then lets me test that knowledge, make mistakes, and see how things actually work.
It may take longer, but I feel that I remember the subject better when I use both methods.
Starting With Statistics
Before moving on to NumPy, Pandas, and machine learning, I studied the fundamentals of statistics.
I did not try to memorise every formula or perform every mathematical calculation by hand. My main goal was to understand the ideas behind the terms: what they represent, why they are used, and how they help us make sense of data.
Python can perform many of the calculations for us. However, getting a result from a library is not the same as understanding what that result means. I believe the important part is knowing why we use a method and how to interpret its output.
Some statistical topics are still difficult, of course. I do not expect to understand everything perfectly on the first attempt. I believe difficult concepts become clearer as we use them in projects, encounter problems, and return to them when necessary.
Does Writing Code Still Matter?
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Today, artificial intelligence can generate code in seconds. It can explain errors, suggest solutions, and even build significant parts of a project.
We will inevitably use these tools, and I think we should.
But I do not believe that knowing how to code has become unnecessary.
Someone who understands programming can recognise when generated code is incorrect, identify the source of an error, and describe the problem more clearly. That knowledge also helps us write better prompts and evaluate the answers we receive.
Two people may use the same AI tool, but their results will not necessarily be equal. The person who understands the underlying logic can ask better questions, notice problems earlier, and adapt the generated solution to the actual project.
For that reason, I still write the code myself while learning. Even if I later ask AI to help me improve or debug it, I first want to understand what the code is doing.
My goal is not to compete with AI by typing faster. It is to build enough knowledge to use AI consciously.
Where I Am Now
I have completed the statistics fundamentals and am currently studying NumPy. Pandas and machine learning will come next, followed eventually by deep learning.
created this Medium account to document that journey honestly. I plan to share the concepts I learn, the mistakes I make, the parts I find difficult, and the small projects I build along the way.
I am not writing as an expert. I am writing as a student who is learning step by step and wants to make that progress visible.
Maybe these posts will help another beginner. At the very least, they will allow me to look back and see how much I have learned.
This is the beginning of that journey.
